prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I ranked B056 fifth in my opening ballot, but reading the other seven ballots has moved it to the top of my list. It is the only shortlisted candidate that every member ranked (eight of eight, five in the top three, two first places), and the arguments for it are of the kind I trust as an instrument builder. The magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping a very large atom number, and this is what took fractional uncertainties to about 1e-18. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by several independent laboratories and metrology institutes, so it passes my test of independent confirmation. It has already opened up real measurements: relativistic redshift across millimetres, constraints on the constancy of fundamental constants, dark-matter couplings, and a likely redefinition of the second. The credit chain is short and consistent across the ballots: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength idea and made the first demonstrations, and Ye drove the performance frontier and the many-body clock physics. A two-name prize is therefore comparatively clean.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and attribution at the edges. The 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control) already cover the comb and the cooling and trapping tools on which the lattice clock rests, so the citation must be worded so that it honours the lattice clock as a distinct invention and not a continuation of earlier prizes. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups made decisive contributions that fall outside a two-name credit, and ion-clock work is a parallel path. I am also not an atomic physicist: I judge this on the evidence of independent confirmation and instrument performance, and I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for the fine points. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so one could argue for waiting for that milestone.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first as a clean case of atomic physics giving a new measurement capability, resting on well-understood atomic structure, with confirmation across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE. She also ranks IceCube sixth and calls recognition somewhat early because the source population is not understood.
responses.response: I agree with the independent-confirmation point, which is what moves me. On IceCube I accept her objection in part. The 2013 diffuse flux is robust, but TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane are evidence-level results, and my own first-place ranking leaned on how mature the discovery claim is. I still think the discovery is solid enough to be a strong alternative, but she is right that the interpretation is not as settled as the clock record, and that weakens my case for putting it first now.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as an original new class of matter protected by band topology, with fifteen years of independent confirmation. He ranks the optical lattice clock only eighth, saying it is outside his core field and that the 2005 prize recognised related precision spectroscopy.
responses.response: I take the topological insulator case seriously and have kept B007 as an alternative. It is conceptually the deepest candidate on the list. I part ways with him on the clock for two reasons. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb, not a lattice of neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, and the 1e-18 result is a different capability. I also note that he defers to AMO colleagues on the clock, as I do on topology. Both of us are therefore outside our field on each other's first choice. The BHZ gap in the B007 credit (Zhang, Bernevig, Hughes) worries me: if the committee cannot settle the credit, the cleaner two-name clock prize is easier to defend.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first and the clock second, praising the clock's conceptual cleanness and mature multi-group confirmation. He ranks IceCube seventh and says the AMANDA pioneers and the earlier Markov, Reines and Learned proposals complicate attribution.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube's attribution is harder than I conveyed in my opening ballot. I named Halzen and Karle as a defensible pair, but Mehlig is right that AMANDA and the earlier proposals leave real credit questions, and the rule of three people cannot reflect a collaboration of this size. That is a further reason not to make IceCube my preferred choice. I also note that he ranks the clock second, so B056 comes close to being a bridge between members who put topology and members who put precision measurement first.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Event Horizon Telescope first as a direct image of light bent around a horizon, consistent with general relativity, and favours Doeleman and Falcke over Zensus.
responses.response: I share his view of the attribution and ranked B022 second for the same instrumental reasons. My reservation is maturity. Mass and spin inferences depend on modelling of the emission, and the Sgr A* image is only a few years old. Kroll ranks it seventh and calls the physics conclusions still being refined. I would keep it as a candidate for a later year rather than push it ahead of a result with 1e-18 confirmed performance.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize do not overlap enough with the lattice clock to reduce its standing.
How to word a citation that credits the lattice clock invention without implying that Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups did not contribute.
Whether to wait for the decision on the redefinition of the second before awarding.
Whether topological insulators (B007) can be given a defensible credit given the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap, since that is the main rival for first place.
Whether IceCube's source-identification results will mature enough in the next few years to settle the interpretation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B056, B007 or B003. I am in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, not IceCube, but IceCube is in my own field of astroparticle physics, so the committee should know that my initial first-place vote came from that closeness to the field.
